title: internal-proxy-connection-pooling-and-backpressure-scrub-notes
content:
Meeting: Architecture scrub — internal proxy connection pooling and backpressure
Date: 2025-02-14 (follow-up 2025-02-20)
Facilitator: Marta Alvarez
Attendees: Ethan Park, Priya Nair, Jonas Müller, Farah Khan, Victor Chen (remote), + async comments from SRE rotation
Purpose: Review design options for connection pooling behavior in the internal north-south/gateway proxy, discuss backpressure and graceful degradation strategies, and agree on rollout/testing plan for Dedicated and Private installs.

Context / problem statement:
- Observed instability during load spikes: backend serving runtime instances see sharp connection bursts causing ephemeral queuing and increased tail latency. Metrics show TCP connection churn and occasional 502s when downstream queues fill.
- Current proxy behavior: per-backend ephemeral connections created on demand, short connection TTL (30s), no shared connection pool for multiplexed HTTP/1.1 clients, limited observability on per-connection queue length.
- Goals: reduce connection churn, provide predictable latency under bursty traffic, enable backpressure and admission control at proxy layer, and keep memory/FD usage bounded for Dedicated capacity customers.

Key constraints:
- Must be compatible with both hosted multi-tenant routing and Dedicated private pools where we cannot change serving runtime quickly.
- Minimal impact to existing HTTP/1.1 clients; we can enable HTTP/2 multiplexing on supported routes but cannot require it.
- Rollout needs quick rollback path and canary timeline (per product rollout policy).

Design options discussed:
1) Long-lived per-backend pooled connections (simple pool)
- Maintain N persistent connections per backend process / slot.
- Pools sized by backend slot count and observed concurrency.
- Pros: low connection churn, predictable FD usage, straightforward failover.
- Cons: risk of head-of-line blocking for HTTP/1.1; requires per-request queuing inside proxy.

2) Protocol-aware multiplexing + adaptive pool
- Use HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3 when available) for intra-cluster links to enable multiplexing and reduce per-request connection overhead. For HTTP/1.1, fall back to a small shared pool + short-lived connections.
- Adaptive pool size driven by 95th percentile concurrent streams and latency SLOs.
- Pros: best steady-state efficiency; degrades smoothly.
- Cons: added complexity (ALPN, TLS reconfiguration, connection upgrade), potential compatibility gaps for legacy runtimes.

3) Explicit backpressure + circuit breaker per-backend slot
- Proxy maintains queue length per slot and exposes admission control at request acceptance time; rejects or queues with exponential backoff when queue length exceeds threshold. Also add a circuit-breaker that opens on sustained high queue latency or error rates.
- Pros: protects downstream, explicit signals for caller, easy to instrument.
- Cons: client-visible rejections; need to tune thresholds per workload.

4) Connection pooling + token-bucket shaping + priority lanes
- Keep a fixed connection pool but implement token-bucket shaping for request acceptance and separate priority lanes for short/interactive vs. long/batch requests.
- Pros: preserves latency for interactive requests; fair treatment for bulk.
- Cons: complexity in classifying requests; requires updated routing metadata (route-level priority).

Observability and metrics additions (must-have for rollout):
- connection_count_per_backend (gauge)
- conn_creation_rate (per 1s)
- avg_conn_age_seconds (histogram)
- per-slot_request_queue_length (gauge)
- per-route_rejection_rate and rejection_reason_tag (counter)
- p95/p99 queue wait time (histogram)
Action: Priya to draft Prometheus metric names and Grafana panels (ETA 2025-02-18).

Performance testing plan:
- Local perf harness: extend existing runtime harness to simulate bursty fanout patterns (short bursts, long tails) — Jonas will add scenarios.
- Canaries: two-phase canary — start with internal infra routes (non-customer-facing) then Dedicated customers with explicit opt-in.
- Load profile: synthesize 10x baseline bursts, with 90% short requests (<100ms processing), 10% long (2–10s) to exercise head-of-line.
Action: Jonas to produce harness scenarios and baseline numbers by 2025-02-20.

Decisions / Consensus reached in session:
- Adopt hybrid approach: enable protocol-aware multiplexing for clusters that support HTTP/2 (default for newly provisioned runtime slots) while implementing a small shared connection pool for HTTP/1.1. Multiplexing rollout gated by health checks. (Decision: green)
- Implement explicit backpressure and a conservative circuit-breaker per-slot. Initial config: queue_limit=128, rejection_mode=reject_with_retryable_error (HTTP 429), circuit_breaker_open_threshold=5% error over 1m with min 50 requests. These numbers are a starting point and will be tuned via canary metrics. (Decision: green)
- Add a lightweight priority lane: header-driven priority (x-rw-priority: low|normal|high). Default to normal unless route metadata marks batch. Will not require major client changes; product teams can opt-in. (Decision: provisional — needs product alignment)

Open questions / unresolved:
- TLS/ALPN compatibility across older Dedicated customers — can we enforce HTTP/2 intra-cluster without negotiation problems? (Action: Victor to audit existing TLS configs, due 2025-02-19)
- How to automatically classify batch vs interactive on legacy routes? (Action: Product/solutions to provide route metadata; Marta to schedule sync with Solutions Eng next week)
- What is acceptable retry behavior from clients upon 429? Need to define idempotency rules and guidance. (Action: Ethan to draft client guidance doc and recommended retry headers by 2025-02-24)

Rollback and failure modes considered:
- If pool/multiplexing causes regressions (increased tail or errors), feature flag to disable at route-level with immediate fallback to previous behavior.
- Circuit-breaker misconfiguration could lead to over-rejection — will ship safe defaults and a fast-release patch window.

Security and resource implications:
- Persistent connections increase memory/FD usage — pool sizes capped and observable.
- Priority lanes could be abused by noisy tenants; require quota enforcement at gateway level.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Phase 0 (spike): instrument metrics + local perf harness updates (Sprint A, owner: Priya/Jonas).
- Phase 1 (engine changes): implement connection pool + basic backpressure and circuit-breaker primitives behind feature flags (Sprint B, owner: Ethan).
- Phase 2 (protocol multiplexing): add HTTP/2 multiplexing with ALPN negotiation where possible, health-check gating (Sprint C, owner: Jonas).
- Phase 3 (canary & rollout): internal canary -> Dedicated opt-in -> broader rollout with monitoring and automatic rollback policies (owner: Marta).
Timeline: aim to have Phase 1 canary by end of Q1 2025 (stretch); adjust based on perf harness results.

Action items (owners + due dates):
- Priya: Prometheus metric naming + Grafana panels (2025-02-18)
- Jonas: Extend perf harness with burst scenarios + baseline (2025-02-20)
- Ethan: Implement circuit-breaker and queue primitives PR + design doc (PR: /pull/378) (2025-02-28)
- Victor: TLS/ALPN compatibility audit (2025-02-19)
- Marta: Schedule solutions eng sync for route metadata & priority lanes (2025-02-21)
- Ethan: Draft client retry guidance doc (2025-02-24)

Notes to self / informal thoughts captured during meeting:
- Consider an adaptive queue_limit that scales with observed per-slot CPU/latency rather than a hard static cap — but that adds oscillation risk.
- Might reuse existing token-bucket quota infra for priority lanes to avoid new quota service.
- When we expose 429s, include structured retry-after and routing metadata to help SDKs make better decisions.

Follow-up meeting: 2025-02-20 10:00 PT (sync on harness results + metric panels)

Edits log: 2025-02-20 appended follow-up notes and clarified decision thresholds.

End of notes.
